                                          Geo3DVQA: Evaluating Vision-Language Models for 3D Geospatial Reasoning
                                                                   from Aerial Imagery

                                                        Mai Tsujimoto1              Junjue Wang1                 Weihao Xuan1,2            Naoto Yokoya1,2,†
                                                                    1                                 2
                                                                        The University of Tokyo           RIKEN AIP          †Corresponding author



                                                                   Abstract




arXiv:2512.07276v2 [cs.CV] 21 Dec 2025
                                                                                                                      The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC)
                                                                                                                  projects an increasing frequency and intensity of climate ex-
                                         Three-dimensional geospatial analysis is critical for appli-             tremes under global warming scenarios [4]. These risks
                                         cations in urban planning, climate adaptation, and environ-              are particularly amplified in urban areas, where three-
                                         mental assessment. Current methodologies depend on costly                dimensional morphology drives local microclimates and
                                         specialized sensors (e.g., LiDAR and multispectral), which               intensifies Urban Heat Island effects [5, 6]. Accurate assess-
                                         restrict global accessibility. Existing sensor-based and rule-           ment of spatial properties, such as sky view factors, building
                                         driven methods further struggle with tasks requiring the                 heights, and urban morphology, is essential for applications
                                         integration of multiple 3D cues, handling diverse queries,               ranging from heat mitigation to disaster risk assessment,
                                         and providing interpretable reasoning. We hereby present                 energy planning, and quality-of-life improvements.
                                         Geo3DVQA, a comprehensive benchmark to evaluate vision-                      Nevertheless, current approaches to three-dimensional
                                         language models (VLMs) in height-aware 3D geospatial                     geospatial analyses face significant accessibility barriers.
                                         reasoning using RGB-only remote sensing imagery. Unlike                  Traditional methods depend on costly specialized sensors
                                         conventional sensor-based frameworks, Geo3DVQA empha-                    such as LiDAR (often costing $100,000 or more) and mul-
                                         sizes realistic scenarios that integrate elevation, sky view fac-        tispectral sensors [7–9]. Beyond acquisition costs, these
                                         tors, and land cover patterns. The benchmark encompasses                 approaches require considerable technical expertise for sen-
                                         110k curated question–answer pairs spanning 16 task cate-                sor operation, data processing workflows, and cross-feature
                                         gories across three complexity levels: single-feature infer-             integration. These limitations restrict advanced geospatial
                                         ence, multi-feature reasoning, and application-level spatial             reasoning to well-funded institutions, creating a substantial
                                         analysis. The evaluation of ten state-of-the-art VLMs high-              accessibility gap in areas where climate adaptation analyses
                                         lights the difficulty of RGB-to-3D reasoning. GPT-4o and                 are most urgently needed.
                                         Gemini-2.5-Flash achieve around 30% overall short-answer                     Conversely, aerial RGB imagery is widely accessible
                                         accuracy, whereas domain-specific fine-tuning of Qwen2.5-                through platforms such as Google Earth and national map-
                                         VL-7B substantially improves performance to nearly 50%,                  ping agencies at minimal or no cost. This contrast naturally
                                         representing a gain of over 20 percentage points compared                leads to the question: Can vision-language models perform
                                         to the base model. Geo3DVQA thus introduces a new fron-                  sophisticated 3D spatial reasoning directly from ubiquitous
                                         tier for scalable, accessible, and interpretable 3D geospatial           RGB imagery alone? We studied their ability to learn and
                                         analyses. The code and data will be released upon publica-               infer imperceptible 3D properties directly from the observ-
                                         tion at https://github.com/mm1129/Geo3DVQA.                              able RGB patterns. Among these properties, the Sky View
                                                                                                                  Factor (SVF) serves as a fundamental metric: it represents
                                                                                                                  the ratio (0–1) of the visible sky from a point and is essential
                                                                                                                  for urban microclimate and solar radiation analysis [10].
                                         1. Introduction                                                              To advance the development of VLMs with robust 3D spa-
                                                                                                                  tial reasoning, we introduce Geo3DVQA, a dedicated VQA
                                         Recent advancements in vision-language models (VLMs) [1–                 (Visual Question Answering) benchmark specifically de-
                                         3] have exhibited noteworthy capabilities in two-dimensional             signed to evaluate height-aware spatial reasoning from aerial
                                         (2D) visual understanding. However, their potential for three-           RGB imagery alone. As shown in Figure 1, our framework
                                         dimensional (3D) spatial reasoning from widely available                 systematically evaluates the models’ ability to extract 3D
                                         RGB imagery remains largely unexplored. This gap is partic-              spatial properties from 2D visual cues. Here we employed
                                         ularly important given the growing importance of 3D geospa-              a concise three-tier taxonomy (single-feature, multi-feature,
                                         tial analysis in addressing contemporary global challenges.              and application-level).

Figure 1. Geo3DVQA Task Taxonomy and Evaluation Framework. Our benchmark comprises 16 task categories organized into three
complexity tiers to evaluate RGB-to-3D spatial reasoning capabilities. Tier 1 (Single-feature): Direct inference of individual properties
across SVF, land cover, and height from RGB patterns. Tier 2 (Multi-feature): Composite reasoning tasks requiring the integration of
multiple spatial attributes (e.g., sky visibility combines SVF with building penalties). Tier 3 (Application-level): Free-form reasoning
for real-world applications in urban planning, renewable energy, landscape analysis, and water accumulation. Ground truth generation
uses multimodal reference data (SVF, DSM, land cover), whereas the models are evaluated using only RGB imagery. The colored regions
indicate the locations of multiple-choice options, with answers highlighted for visualization.

aware reasoning (e.g., relative comparisons and bin-level
distinctions). It is designed to be realistic for RGB-only                                                             2. Related Work

2.2. Inferring 3D Properties from RGB
For monocular height estimation, a rich line of work
estimates the height or DSM from single-view imagery.                    that were curated at 1 m spatial resolution, covering 10 land
IM2HEIGHT [25] pioneered learning-based height regres-                   cover classes.
sion from monocular images, while subsequent approaches                  Spatial data processing. Digital Surface Models (DSM)
leveraged shadow geometry and sun elevation for building                 provide elevation information vital for spatial analysis [29,
height estimation [14] and extended to IM2ELEVATION-                     30]. From the DSM data, we computed the SVF values us-
style pipelines for DSM/height prediction [13]. Most of                  ing the Urban Multi-scale Environmental Predictor (UMEP)
these methods target continuous value map generation with                toolkit with ray casting [10]. This approach is widely
explicit height supervision.                                             adopted in urban climate analysis and demonstrates strong
    The SVF can be delivered either from DSM/LiDAR                       agreement with fisheye imagery and high-resolution 3D mod-
or street-view fisheye imagery with semantic segmenta-                   els (R2 >0.91, RMSE ≈ 0.07) [26, 31, 32]. Our processing
tion [10, 26]. Estimating continuous SVF from RGB data                   pipeline (Fig. 2) aligned these multimodal reference data
alone is a challenge. Some attempts have been made to                    (i.e., SVF, elevation, and segmentation data), extracted spa-
use satellite shadow cues [27], but robust inference gener-              tial indicators, and generated question–answer pairs.
ally relies on 3D data. Furthermore, practical applications                  Although the SVF mainly quantifies vertical openness,
require an integrated understanding of multiple spatial prop-            it can overestimate perceived openness because horizontal
erties beyond isolated SVF estimation. This need motivated               obstructions are not fully captured [6, 32, 33]. To address
our investigation into VLMs’ ability to infer height-aware               this limitation, we employed a composite sky visibility metric
properties from RGB patterns. Our evaluation bridges 2D                  that integrates SVF with land cover information, providing
semantic understanding and 3D geometric reasoning through                a more realistic representation of perceived openness [34–
a language-based assessment without specialized sensors.                 36]. The reliability of these metrics and the derived results
                                                                         was checked via statistical validation and multimodal visual

Figure 4. The shortened examples of Tier-3 free-form Q&A with RGB input and reference for ground truth. Statistics were first calculated
from the reference modalities (SVF, DSM, segmentation) and input into GPT-4.1-mini to generate answers corresponding to pre-defined
categories. These answers were validated by cross-checking them against the reference statistics using GPT-5. Q&As that passed the
validation are then verified by humans, and the final Q&A pairs are used for evaluation.

Table 2. Aggregated Evaluation Across Major Categories. Accuracy (%) and free-form scores (1–5 scale) in the last two columns. SVF,
Height, and Land Use/LC are single-feature inference (T1). Multi represents multi-feature inference (T2). Overall covers all short-answer
categories (T1+T2). Free-form evaluation (T3) uses rubric-based scoring for structured-reasoning tasks. FT(10 K) and FT(100 K) in
the result tables denote fine-tuning with 10 K and 100 K instruction-tuning samples, respectively. ‘FT–Base’ indicates the performance
improvements achieved by fine-tuning Qwen-2.5-VL on 100K Q&As (‘Qwen2.5-VL-7B FT (100K)’) compared to the baseline results
(‘Qwen2.5-VL-7B Base’).
*Format errors (repeated questions without answers): o4-mini 47.2%, Gemini-2.5-Flash 16.3%, others <2%.

                                                                          4.2. Detailed Analysis
orously assess the value of the end-to-end VLM approach,
we conducted additional experiments using inputs other than               VLM spatial reasoning challenges and architectural con-
RGB. First, we evaluated a configuration with access to var-              straints. The results point to the fundamental limitations
ious ground truth modalities (DSM/SVF/segmentation) at                    of current vision-language model architectures in spatial
inference. Using only the necessary modalities for each ques-             tasks requiring coordinate-level understanding. For instance,
tion tended to improve category-specific accuracy. The best               VLMs achieve only 32.7% accuracy in the visibility range,
overall accuracy reached 57.4% (Height Inference: 69.25%)                 which highlights the constraints of patch-based vision en-
with agent-style routing, which selected the necessary modal-             coders. Even with advanced high-resolution techniques such
ities for each question. Second, we evaluated a two-stage                 as AnyRes (LLaVA-OneVision) and dynamic resolution pro-
pipeline that used three pretrained UNet-based monocular                  cessing (Qwen2.5-VL), images are still partitioned into dis-
predictors on GeoNRW to estimate the DSM/SVF/segmen-                      crete patches rather than interpreted in continuous coordi-
tation from RGB, followed by agent-style inference. This                  nates [40, 42, 43]. This leads to systematic errors, such as

A.1.5. Question Generation Framework
                                                                     processing workflow follows these steps:
Our question-generation framework incorporates several key           1. Statistical feature compilation into a structured JSON-
design principles to ensure systematic coverage of reason-              style format from SVF, DSM, segmentation, and RGB
ing capabilities while maintaining diversity and practical              inputs
relevance.                                                           2. Template-based question generation using pre-defined
Difficulty Stratification Methodology. Questions were                   categories and base prompts
systematically categorized into difficulty levels through a          3. Answer generation based on statistical evidence and do-
multi-stage classification process. The stratification frame-           main knowledge using GPT-4.1-mini and human expert
work ensures a broad evaluation of model capabilities across            prompt refinement
different complexity levels, from basic spatial queries to           4. Iterative refinement with an LLM-based verifier
complex multi-feature reasoning tasks and complete deep                 that checks answers against the SVF/DSM/segmenta-
reasoning analyses.                                                     tion/RGB statistics and a 2×2 multimodal panel, com-
Modality-Specific Design Principles. Each task category                 bined with rule-based consistency checks
is designed to leverage specific data modalities effectively         5. Human expert validation on a sampled subset for accuracy
(SVF, DSM, RGB, and semantic segmentation), ensuring                    and consistency with colorized SVF, DSM, RGB, and
that multi-feature integration provides meaningful advan-               segmentation data
tages over single-feature approaches. The design process fol-
lowed established geospatial analysis methodologies while            A.1.7. Quality Assurance and Validation
adapting them for vision-language model evaluation.                  Bias Mitigation Implementation. Our generation frame-

lished methodologies from prior VLM benchmarking re-                 gies to ensure a fair evaluation across different spatial pat-
search, we employed a systematic template-based approach             terns and urban environments. The bias mitigation process
with manually curated question templates for each category.          includes:

Sky View Factor and Sky Visibility Methodology. The                                                                                cal openness to incorporate the geometric sightline length
Sky View Factor (SVF) quantifies the hemispherical sky                                                                             across the terrain. Standard viewshed analysis on DSMs
fraction visible from a given point. This geometric metric                                                                         models horizon blocking and line of sight constraints. This
has become foundational in urban climatology [26, 65] with                                                                         approach is widely used for environmental monitoring and
applications covering energy efficiency [37, 66] and solar                                                                         path planning [69].
potential analysis [27]. Our computational methodology fol-                                                                            Landscape visibility surveys emphasize that horizon struc-
lows established geometric algorithms for hemispherical sky                                                                        ture and local relief shape visible extent and perceived view
visibility calculations, incorporating digital surface model                                                                       quality [70]. These studies recommend multi criteria formu-
data for accurate obstruction modeling.                                                                                            lations that combine viewshed extent with openness proxies.
    However, SVF captures primarily vertical openness. Re-                                                                         We therefore mix the viewshed (60%), local SVF context
cent reviews note that it may overestimate perceived open-                                                                         (25%), and terrain roughness (15%) to balance the raw sight-
ness when lateral obstructions are significant [6, 32, 33].                                                                        line reach, occlusion likelihood, and terrain comfort.
Street canyon studies link lower SVF values to stronger hori-                                                                      Urban density. Urban density is characterized by coverage
zon obstruction and heat island intensity [5, 61]. Yet lateral                                                                     and volume based metrics. The building coverage ratio
barriers such as building walls, tree belts, and near field                                                                        (BCR) and floor area ratio (FAR) are canonical in urban
structures can block sky access even where SVF remains                                                                             planning and daylight regulation. We complement these
high.                                                                                                                              with an SVF component (1-\overline {\mathrm {SVF}}) that captures enclosure
    We therefore model sky visibility as a composite measure                                                                       from local massing. This term is clamped to zero in nature
governed by SVF but modulated by local land cover and                                                                              dominant regions to avoid conflating canopy cover with
building configuration. This approach better approximates                                                                          urban density.

E.0.2. Dataset Statistics and Visualization
E.0.3. Model Size Constraints and Future Scaling
All local experiments were bounded to models with at most
10 B parameters owing to server memory limits for both
training and inference. This constraint influences our archi-
tectural choices and may understate the attainable ceiling
for elevation- and SVF-aware reasoning. Future work will
investigate the scaling behavior with respect to free-form co-
herence, format compliance under constrained decoding, and
multi-image conditioning for improved coordinate fidelity.

E.0.4. Input/Output Normalization and Examples
Input/Output Normalization Rules.
• Coordinates and Regions: See the Coordinate Guide for
  normalized coordinate definitions and region format.
• Output labels: fixed vocabulary for LU/LC; case-sensitive
  matching.
• Numerical outputs: clipped to valid ranges and rounded to
  specified precision.

                         Listing 2. FT example: Urban Development (QID 1: koeln 364 5633 dem)
Question ID: 1 (koeln_364_5633_dem)
Question (excerpt): Analyze the potential of this area for urban development.

Ground truth sections (excerpt):
<OBSERVATION>Built environment coverage was 20.8%, with vegetation dominating at 66.5% (agricultural
    ,→ 57.4%, natural vegetation 9.2%). Mean SVF is 0.915. Elevation ranges 43.4-76.8 m (delta 33.4 m),
    ,→ relative variation 0.60. Urbanization level was 2/5 and the spatial diversity index was 1.320.
    ,→ The highest sky accessibility was in the middle center, and the best scenic quality was in the
    ,→ middle right.</OBSERVATION>
<CONCLUSION>Low building density and high SVF support comfortable expansion; prioritize top-center
    ,→ infrastructure; preserve middle-right scenic zones; leverage elevation variation for diversified
    ,→ fabric; maintain vegetation >50% with green corridors.</CONCLUSION>

Model sections (FT prediction):
<OBSERVATION> The built environment coverage was 21.5%, with residential areas dominating at 18.7%.
    ,→ Agricultural land covers 69.1% of the area, whereas natural vegetation is minimal at 0.1%. Mean
    ,→ SVF is 0.851. Elevation ranges 48.1-60.1 m (delta 12.0 m), terrain complexity 0.24. The highest
    ,→ sky accessibility top-left; bottom-right offers the best development suitability.</OBSERVATION>
<CONCLUSION>Maintain low building density to preserve scenic quality and sky openness. Prioritize
    ,→ bottom-right development, enhance green corridors by increasing natural vegetation, and improve
    ,→ infrastructure connectivity while maintaining a safe elevation.</CONCLUSION>

                     Listing 3. FT example: Landscape Analysis (QID 7: guetersloh 454 5748 dem)
Question ID: 7 (guetersloh_454_5748_dem)
Question (excerpt): Analyze the overall landscape in terms of sky visibility, terrain, and land cover.

Ground truth sections (excerpt):
<OBSERVATION>Natural vegetation 32.5%, built 7.8%, forest 28.8%, agriculture 56.7%. Elevation
    ,→ 67.9-100.7 m (mean 76.5 m, delta 32.8 m, var. 0.43). The mean sky openness was 0.783
    ,→ (0.011-1.000); highest top-right. Spatial diversity index: 1.174; urbanization: 1/5; scenic
    ,→ quality: 0.727.</OBSERVATION>
<CONCLUSION>Natural-agricultural balance with low built density, moderate relief supports connectivity,
    ,→ top-right openness enhances solar and visual quality, conserve forest patches, and focus
    ,→ development top-left to minimize fragmentation.</CONCLUSION>

Model sections (FT prediction):
<OBSERVATION>Natural vegetation 12.5% (forest 11.6%); agriculture 79.8%; built 0.1%. Elevation
    ,→ 100.1-141.1 m (mean 116.1 m, delta 41.0 m, var. 0.35). The mean sky openness was 0.811
    ,→ (0.011-1.000); highest top-left. The Shannon diversity was 0.641. Scenic quality 0.711.</
    ,→ OBSERVATION>
<CONCLUSION>Agriculture-dominant landscape with limited urbanization; terrain variation supports
    ,→ connectivity; high sky openness enhances visual quality; conserve forest patches to maintain
    ,→ biodiversity.</CONCLUSION>

                        Listing 7. Point Selection (Visibility range with scoring and coordinates)
System: You are a precise geospatial assistant. Answer concisely.
User: Which location has the most comprehensive sight lines?
Hint: Areas with good visibility typically have a high sky view factor and fewer obstacles in the line


                                                            30
    ,→ of sight.
Scoring method: Locations were scored solely based on viewshed distance analysis (60%), Sky View Factor
    ,→ (25%), and terrain roughness variation (15%). Higher scores indicate a better visibility range
    ,→ with longer line-of-sight distances.
Coordinate system: Each point is specified by (x, y) coordinates as percentages of the image dimensions,
    ,→ where (0, 0) represents the top-left corner. ’x’ represents the horizontal position (from left
    ,→ to right), and ’y’ represents the vertical position (from top to bottom).
Please choose from:
Point (75.3%, 41.8%)
Point (1.9%, 46.7%)
Point (34.7%, 50.6%)
Point (4.2%, 84.8%)
Answer format: Point (x.x%, y.y%)

                                                      31
G. Data and Code Availability
Release scope and licensing constraints. We are commit-
ted to maximizing reproducibility within the GeoNRW data
licensing restrictions. Upon publication, we plan to release
the following:
Publicly released components (unrestricted access):
• Question–answer pairs with image identifiers (110k items)
   and splits
• Evaluation scripts and rubric-based assessors for free-form
   scoring
• Fine-tuned model checkpoints (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) and
   training code
• Documentation of task definitions, metrics, and validation
   procedures
Access-restricted components (require GeoNRW license):
• Raw aerial RGB imagery (1 m) and raw DSM/segmenta-
   tion rasters
    A project page with links to the repository and model
weights will be announced on our GitHub repository.
